newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony opens new video game war front in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Sony opens new video game war front in Asia.

text.p: Sony Corp opened another front in the global video game war on Tuesday when it said it would introduce a new version of its PlayStation game machine in Asia a day after slashing prices on it in the United States.

The company's game unit, Sony Computer Entertainment Inc, unveiled a new version of its 32-bit PlayStation designed for the Asian market outside Japan and said it would hit the market in mid-March and retail for $HK2,580 ($333).
A Sony Computer Entertainment spokesman said the company hopes to sell 10,000 PlayStations in Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia by the end of June.
But analysts said that goal may be too conservative.
"Considering the rising average incomes in the region, the sales target is fairly conservative," said Akira Namekawa, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute.

In the long term, the region will become a significant part of the global video game market, and Nintendo Co Ltd and Sega Enterprises Ltd will likely follow Sony in taking an aggressive stance there, he said.
But a Nintendo spokesman said on Tuesday that it currently does not plan to mass market its 64-bit game machine, Nintendo 64, in Asia.
"We only sell a negligible amount of our game machines in Hong Kong and other parts of Asia. The market is not profitable as it is already flooded with unauthorised copies of game software," he said.
A Sega spokeswoman said it had been selling its 32-bit Sega Saturn game machine in Asia since it was introduced in late 1994, but did not have any sales figures for the region.
Sony's new Asian model will be more than twice as expensive as the regular PlayStation sold in the United States, which now retails for $149 after a 25 percent price cut on Monday.
The Sony Computer Entertainment spokesman said the new model to be sold only in Asia will cost more because it can also play video compact discs.

Sony sent a jolt through the U.S. video game market on Monday with its price cut. It also cut the price of all of its new software titles for the game machine to $49, making them cheaper than many of its rivals' offerings.
Although the price cut makes the PlayStation $50 cheaper than the Nintendo 64, Nintendo said on Monday it had no plans to cut the price of its 64-bit game machine for now.
The next-generation offerings from Sony, Nintendo and Sega have much better graphics and sound than their predecessors, but have been too expensive for most households, analysts said.
With the price cut, the number of PlayStation units in the United States could almost double to six million by Christmas, from about 3.4 million at present, U.S. analysts said.
PlayStation currently has a nearly 50 percent share of the worldwide market for game machines of 32 bits or more, while Sega holds 32.3 percent and Nintendo 18 percent. ($1=7.74 Hong Kong dollars)
